title: India's Data Centre Capacity Quadruples to 1,575 MW as AI Demand Accelerates
excerpt: The government told Parliament that data centre capacity has grown more than fourfold since 2020, driven by artificial intelligence and high-performance computing, with nuclear energy and advanced cooling technologies supporting sustainable expansion.
body:
• India's data centre capacity has grown from 375 MW in 2020 to approximately 1,575 MW in 2026, a more-than-fourfold increase driven by AI and high-performance computing
  • Over 38,000 GPUs have been onboarded through 14 empanelled providers under the IndiaAI Mission, available to startups and researchers at ₹65 per hour — roughly one-third of global rates
  • The SHANTI Act, recently passed by Parliament, positions nuclear energy including small modular reactors as a power source for AI infrastructure
  • Morgan Stanley projects Indian data centre capacity could surge nearly sixfold to 10.5 GW by FY2031, with AI workloads accounting for 6.8 GW

India's data centre capacity has increased more than fourfold from 375 MW in 2020 to approximately 1,575 MW, the government informed the Lok Sabha on Wednesday, attributing the rapid expansion to surging demand from artificial intelligence and high-performance computing workloads.

The Numbers Behind the Surge

Minister of State for Electronics and Information Technology Jitin Prasada provided the figures in a written reply, describing the growth as part of the government's broader push to build a sovereign AI ecosystem. Mumbai and Navi Mumbai account for the largest share of operational capacity at 790 MW, followed by Chennai at 305 MW, Bengaluru at 182 MW, Hyderabad at 152 MW, and Delhi-NCR/Noida at 76 MW.

The growth trajectory is expected to steepen. A Morgan Stanley report published in May projected that Indian data centre capacity could surge nearly sixfold to approximately 10.5 GW by FY2031, with AI workloads alone accounting for roughly 6.8 GW of the projected capacity. The investment bank estimated an industrial capital expenditure pipeline of around $60 billion linked to incremental data centre capacity.

India's incremental electricity demand between 2025 and 2030 is expected to be 32% higher than that of the United States, according to a separate analysis by India Capital Management, with approximately one-fifth of the increase attributable to AI-related workloads.

Subsidised AI Compute at Scale

The government's IndiaAI Mission has operationalised a compute access programme that has onboarded over 38,000 GPUs through 14 empanelled service providers and data centres. These are available to startups, researchers, and academic institutions at a subsidised average rate of ₹65 per hour — roughly one-third of the global average cost for comparable compute power.

Prasada said the IndiaAI Mission aims to build a sovereign AI stack comprising compute capacity, foundational models, and indigenous applications, with a focus on democratising access to AI technologies. The programme's data centres are located across Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Noida, and Jamnagar.

Nuclear Power and Green Infrastructure

The government highlighted multiple measures to ensure the expansion remains environmentally sustainable. These include the Green Energy Open Access Rules, the Green Energy Corridor Scheme, the National Green Hydrogen Mission, and the Solar Park Scheme.

The most notable policy development is the recently enacted SHANTI Act — Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India — which is designed to strengthen reliable clean power for sectors such as AI and data centres, including the future deployment of small modular and micro nuclear reactors.

"The rapid growth of AI and high-performance computing is driving increasing demand for data centre capacity in the country."

— Government reply to the Lok Sabha

The Bureau of Indian Standards has published standards covering Power Usage Effectiveness, Carbon Usage Effectiveness, Cooling Efficiency Ratio, and Water Usage Effectiveness for data centres. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency has notified energy conservation building codes prescribing efficiency and water conservation norms relevant to data centre operations.

Advanced Cooling and Industry Response

The government noted that the industry is adopting advanced cooling technologies to reduce power and water consumption. These include direct-to-chip liquid cooling, adiabatic cooling, immersion cooling, and closed-loop liquid cooling systems, alongside high-density rack deployments to support AI workloads efficiently.

Electricity demand from data centres alone is estimated to reach 13.56 GW by 2031-32, according to the Ministry of Power. India's national transmission infrastructure is being expanded to meet this growing demand.

The data centre boom has attracted global hyperscalers. Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have all announced significant India investments in recent months. Four submarine cable systems are currently under commissioning at various cable landing stations by telecom service providers, including India Europe Xpress by Reliance Jio, SEA-ME-WE-6 and 2Africa by Bharti Airtel, and the Raman Cable by Sify Technologies.

Policy measures such as data localisation requirements and infrastructure status for data centres are accelerating capital formation and positioning India as a regional hub for cloud and digital services — a trend Morgan Stanley expects to deepen as geopolitical realignments and regulatory pushes catalyse a multi-year investment cycle.
nri_angle: India's data centre surge is creating opportunities for diaspora tech professionals in cloud infrastructure and AI, while the country's subsidised GPU access at one-third of global rates positions it as a competitive destination for AI ventures.
author: Diaspora Desk
